text: In 1803, the United States doubled in size. Over night, it paid about three cents an acre. In 1867, it bottled land more than twice the size of Texas. People called it a folly. And in 1946, it secretly tried to buy the biggest island on Earth, with gold. America didn't only grow by fighting. It grew by shopping. This is every time America bought land, and at the end you'll see which deal was the best and which one was the most expensive. Part 1 The deal of the century It's 1803. The United States is a young country squeezed against the Atlantic. Everything west of the Mississippi River belongs to France, and France belongs to one man, Napoleon. America only wants one city, New Orleans. Every farmer in the West ships his crops down the Mississippi, and New Orleans is the door to the sea. So, President Thomas Jefferson sends his diplomats to Paris, with permission to spend up to $10 million for New Orleans and a piece of Florida. But Napoleon has a problem. His army has just lost a war in Haiti and a new war with Britain is coming. He needs money. Fast. So the French make an offer nobody expected. Napoleon's minister asks the Americans, what would you give for the whole of Louisiana? Why buy a city when you can buy everything? 828,000 square miles for $15 million. three about $3 an acre, with one signature, the United States doubled in size. This land would later become all or part of 15 states from Louisiana to Montana. One of the American diplomats, Robert Livingston, said it was the noblest work of their whole lives. And here's the twist. America didn't have the cash. So it borrowed from two banks, bearing brothers in London and hoping company in Amsterdam. Translation, British bankers helped pay Napoleon just as he went back to war with Britain. Part 2. The South, the war, and a railroad. Next on the list, Florida. In 1819, Spain is too weak to hold it and hands it over in the Adam's own East Treaty. America doesn't even write Spain a check. Instead, it agrees to pay up to five million dollars of claims that American citizens had against Spain. Then comes the biggest and most controversial. In 1846, the United States goes to war with Mexico. Two years later, the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo hands over about 500,000 square miles, California, Nevada, Utah, and large parts of Arizona, New Mexico, and Colorado. In return, the United States pays Mexico $15 million. A purchase, yes, but signed after a war. Counting Texas, Mexico lost about half of its territory, and the timing is unbelievable. On January 24th, 1848, gold is found at Sutter's Mill in California. Nine days later, the treaty is signed. Mexico had just given away the land of the gold rush without knowing it. But the border still wasn't finished. Look at this strip at the bottom of Arizona and New Mexico. In 1853, the United States buys it for $10 million. Why? A railroad. Engineers said the best southern route to California ran through this flat desert. It's called the Gadsden Purchase. The city of Tucson came with it. And it's why the border looks like this today. Part 3. Sewer its icebox 1867 Russia owns a giant piece of North America, Alaska, but it's far from the Russian capital, hard to defend, and Russia fears it could lose it to Britain anyway. So it offers to sell. The American Secretary of State, William Sewward, negotiates through the night and the deal is signed at 4 in the morning. The price? $7.2 million for 586,000 square miles, about 2 cents an acre. Alaska is more than twice the size of Texas. Put it on top of the lower 48, and with its islands, it stretches almost from coast to coast. But back then, critics laughed. Newspapers called it Seward's Icebox. Some even called it Wall Russia. Then came gold in the 1890s. And in 1968, the biggest oil field in North America at Prudobae. The icebox was a treasure chest. And one more thing. From Little Diamonde Island in Alaska, you can see Russia. Big DioMede is only about two and a half miles away. Part 4. The Most Expensive Acre. Not every deal was cheap. In 1917 during the First World War, the United States buys three small Caribbean islands from Denmark, St. Thomas, St. John and St. Croix. Today, they're the US Virgin Islands. The price? $25 million in gold. For about 134 square miles. That's almost $300 an acre compared to Louisiana about 10,000 times more expensive. Why pay so much? Fear. Washington worried that Germany could take the islands and use them as a submarine base close to the Panama Canal. And there's one purchase America later let go. In 1898, after a war with Spain, the United States paid Spain $20 million for the Philippines, more than 7,000 islands. In 1946, the Philippines became independent. Same story in Panama. In 1904 the United States paid $10 million to control a strip of land 10 miles wide to build the Panama Canal. In 1999 it handed it back. Part 5. The One That Got Away. And then there's Greenland. In 1946 President Harry Truman's government secretly offered Denmark $100 million in gold for the biggest island on Earth. Denmark said no. Greenland is huge, about 836,000 square miles, bigger than the entire Louisiana purchase. But only about 56,000 people live there. In 2019, and again in 2025, the idea came back. And the answer from Denmark and Greenland was the same. Greenland is not for sale. Why does America want it so much? Look at the map. Greenland sits between North America and Europe on the shortest route over the Arctic. Translation? Whoever holds Greenland watches the top of the world. So, which deal was the best? At about two cents an acre, Alaska was the cheapest. Louisiana doubled the country for three cents, and the Virgin Islands cost almost $300 an acre. Added all up, and more than half of today's United States came from deals that ended with a payment. A city that became half a continent, a desert bought for a railroad, an icebox full of gold, and an island that said no. Which deal would you have made? And should America still try to buy Greenland?
